dedupe_keys.name: healthcare waste management services in 2 002 health facilities of 14 low and middle income countries determinants of access

description: This case study examines what explains whether health facilities in low- and middle-income countries have safe waste management. The authors, from the Water Institute at the University of North Carolina, published it as an open-access journal article using facility surveys from World Vision programmes. Multilevel models related six elements of safe waste management, such as a functional incinerator, bins for segregation, and proper sharps and infectious waste disposal, to facility and country predictors across 2,002 healthcare facilities in 14 countries. The article is free under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial licence. Caveats: facilities come from programme areas, not national samples, survey answers are observational, and associations are not causal. Only 8 percent of facilities had basic waste management; facilities with working electricity had higher odds of a functional incinerator (odds ratio 1.26), safe segregation bins (1.28) and proper sharps disposal (1.48); following operations and maintenance protocols helped; and a higher national water, sanitation and hygiene budget share of GDP was associated with better services. Simulation uses: parameterising healthcare waste service gaps and their dependence on electricity in interdependency and resilience models of health systems. Related records: the WHO harmonized health facility assessment (data-who-harmonized-health-facility-assessment-hhfa) and the DHS service provision assessment (data-dhs-service-provision-assessment) collect comparable facility data.
